units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Factorising expressions
units.topic: Common factors and difference of squares
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Mathematics, Term 1: Algebraic expressions (products of binomials; factorise by taking out a common factor; difference of two squares; trinomials)
units.intention: Today I am factorising expressions, which is expanding in reverse.
units.prompt: How do you check that you factorised correctly?

lesson.say: Expanding three times x plus two gives three x plus six. Factorising goes backwards: three x plus six becomes three times x plus two.
lesson.html:
3(x + 2)→⇄→3x + 6

Factorise means write as a product.

lesson.say: Find the highest common factor of all the terms. In four x squared plus eight x, the common factor is four x. So it is four x times x plus two.
lesson.html:
4x² + 8x→= 4x(x + 2)

Take out the highest common factor.

lesson.say: A squared minus b squared always factorises to a minus b times a plus b. So x squared minus nine is x minus three times x plus three.
lesson.html:
a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)→x² − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3)

Look for two perfect squares with a minus between them.

example.q: Factorise 5a² − 15a.
steps: Both terms contain 5 and a.
The highest common factor is 5a.

questions.q: Factorise: 6x + 12
Factorise: y² − 25
Factorise: 3m² + 9m
questions.explain: 3m² + 9m = 3m(m + 3). The other forms are not fully factorised.

questions.q: Which can be factorised as a difference of two squares?
Expand to check: (x − 4)(x + 4) = ?
questions.explain: The middle terms cancel, leaving x² − 16.

units.parent: Your child factorised algebraic expressions using common factors and the difference of two squares.
units.teacher: Shows factorising by highest common factor and difference of two squares, and checking by expansion.
units.done: Factorising writes an expression as a product. Always check by expanding.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Straight-line graphs
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Mathematics, Term 3: Graphs (draw and interpret linear graphs; gradient and y-intercept; y = mx + c)
units.intention: Today I am reading the gradient and y-intercept of a straight line.
units.prompt: What does a steeper line tell you?

lesson.say: Every straight line can be written as y equals m x plus c. The number m is the gradient, the steepness. The number c is where the line crosses the y-axis.
lesson.html:
y = mx + c→m: gradient→c: y-intercept

For y = 2x + 1, the gradient is 2 and the line crosses the y-axis at 1.

lesson.say: For y equals two x plus one: when x is zero, y is one. When x is one, y is three. When x is two, y is five. Each step right, y goes up by two.
lesson.html:
x: 0, 1, 2→y: 1, 3, 5

y goes up by the gradient each time x goes up by 1.

lesson.say: A positive gradient slopes up from left to right. A negative gradient slopes down. A gradient of zero is flat.
lesson.html:
m > 0: up ↗→m < 0: down ↘→m = 0: flat →

A bigger number means a steeper line.

example.q: A taxi charges R10 plus R5 per kilometre. Write it as y = mx + c.
steps: The fixed amount is R10. That is where the line starts: c = 10.
Each kilometre adds R5: m = 5.

questions.q: What is the gradient of y = 3x − 4?
hints: m is the number with x.

questions.q: Where does y = 2x + 7 cross the y-axis?
questions.explain: c = 7, so it crosses at (0; 7).

questions.q: For y = 4x + 1, what is y when x = 3?
Which line slopes down from left to right?
questions.explain: A negative gradient slopes down.

questions.q: A phone contract costs R99 a month plus R1 per minute. Which equation fits?
hints: R1 per minute is the gradient.

units.parent: Your child read the gradient and y-intercept of straight-line graphs and used them in real situations.
units.teacher: Shows identifying gradient and y-intercept from y = mx + c, substitution, sign of gradient, and modelling a context.
units.done: In y = mx + c, m is the steepness and c is where the line starts.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Probability
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Mathematics, Term 4: Probability (sample space; relative frequency; probability of simple events; compare predicted and actual results)
units.intention: Today I am calculating the chance that something will happen.
units.prompt: Why don't experiments always match the predicted probability?

lesson.say: Probability is how likely something is, from zero, impossible, to one, certain. A half means it is equally likely to happen or not.
lesson.html:
0 impossible→½ even chance→1 certain

Probability can be a fraction, decimal or percentage.

lesson.say: Probability equals the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes. The chance of rolling a six on a die is one out of six.
lesson.html:
P = favourable ÷ total→P(6) = 1/6

The list of all outcomes is the sample space.

lesson.say: If you flip a coin 20 times, you expect about 10 heads, but you might get 12. The more times you try, the closer the result gets to the prediction.
lesson.html:
Predicted: 10 heads→Actual: 12 heads

Relative frequency = how often it happened ÷ number of trials.

example.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue sweets. What is the probability of picking red?
steps: Favourable outcomes: 3 red.
Total: 3 + 5 = 8.

questions.q: What is the probability of getting heads when you flip a fair coin?
questions.explain: P(heads) = 1/2.

questions.q: What is the probability of rolling an even number on a die?
Which event is impossible?
options: Rolling a 7 on a normal die
questions.explain: A normal die has no 7, so P = 0.

questions.q: A spinner has 4 equal parts: 2 green, 1 red, 1 yellow. What is P(green)?
Lungi flips a coin 50 times and gets 29 heads. What is the relative frequency of heads?
questions.explain: Relative frequency = 29/50 = 0,58.

options: Thinking of real dice and coins

units.parent: Your child calculated probabilities and compared predicted results with actual results.
units.teacher: Shows determining sample spaces, calculating theoretical probability and relative frequency.
units.done: Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Reading an argument
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 English Home Language: Reading and Viewing; Writing and Presenting (argumentative and discursive texts: claims, evidence, counter-arguments, conclusion)
units.intention: Today I am analysing how an argument is built.
units.prompt: Which side of the argument convinces you more, and why?
units.passage:
Should Cellphones Be Allowed in Class? (a 2to.iQ article)

Across South Africa, schools are debating whether learners should be allowed to use cellphones in class. Some schools ban them completely, while others allow them for learning.

Supporters say phones give learners access to dictionaries, calculators and videos that explain hard topics. For learners without books at home, a phone may be their main way to research.

However, many teachers say phones distract learners. Notifications interrupt concentration, and some learners use social media during lessons. Studies in several countries have found that test results improved after phones were banned.

There are also safety concerns. Phones can be stolen, and cyberbullying can continue during school hours.

Some schools have found a middle path: phones stay in bags unless the teacher asks learners to use them for a task. This keeps the benefits while reducing distraction.

lesson.say: Read the article, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Should Cellphones Be Allowed in Class? (a 2to.iQ article)

Across South Africa, schools are debating whether learners should be allowed to use cellphones in class. Some schools ban them completely, while others allow them for learning.

Supporters say phones give learners access to dictionaries, calculators and videos that explain hard topics. For learners without books at home, a phone may be their main way to research.

However, many teachers say phones distract learners. Notifications interrupt concentration, and some learners use social media during lessons. Studies in several countries have found that test results improved after phones were banned.

There are also safety concerns. Phones can be stolen, and cyberbullying can continue during school hours.

Some schools have found a middle path: phones stay in bags unless the teacher asks learners to use them for a task. This keeps the benefits while reducing distraction.

lesson.say: A claim is a point someone argues. Evidence supports it: facts, examples, statistics or expert views. A claim without evidence is weak.
lesson.html:
Claim→→→Evidence→→→Explanation

Ask: what is the proof?

lesson.say: This article is discursive. It presents both sides fairly. An argumentative text takes one side and argues for it, but should still answer the other side.
lesson.html:
Discursive: both sides→Argumentative: one side

A strong argument deals with the counter-argument.

example.q: Which sentence gives evidence for banning phones?
steps: Look for facts, not just opinions.
Studies found test results improved after bans.
That is evidence from research.

questions.q: Is this article discursive or argumentative?
hints: It gives views for and against.
questions.explain: It presents both sides fairly, so it is discursive.

questions.q: Which is an argument FOR phones in class?
options: Learners can use dictionaries and calculators
questions.explain: Access to learning tools supports allowing phones.

questions.q: What does the word However signal in paragraph 3?
options: A change to the other side
questions.explain: However introduces the opposing view.

questions.q: What is the middle path the article suggests?
options: Phones stay in bags unless needed for a task
questions.explain: Phones stay away unless the teacher asks for them.

questions.q: Which would make the argument stronger?
options: Naming the studies and their results
questions.explain: Specific, checkable evidence strengthens an argument.

reflect.q: How did you analyse the argument?

units.parent: Your child analysed how an argument is built with claims, evidence and counter-arguments.
units.teacher: Shows distinguishing discursive from argumentative text, identifying claims, evidence, discourse markers and evaluating strength.
units.done: Strong arguments use evidence and answer the other side.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Writing a summary
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 English Home Language: Reading and Viewing (summarise a text: select main points, use own words, keep to a word limit)
units.intention: Today I am learning to pick out main points and summarise in my own words.
units.prompt: How did you decide what to leave out?
units.passage:
Should Cellphones Be Allowed in Class? (a 2to.iQ article)

Across South Africa, schools are debating whether learners should be allowed to use cellphones in class. Some schools ban them completely, while others allow them for learning.

Supporters say phones give learners access to dictionaries, calculators and videos that explain hard topics. For learners without books at home, a phone may be their main way to research.

However, many teachers say phones distract learners. Notifications interrupt concentration, and some learners use social media during lessons. Studies in several countries have found that test results improved after phones were banned.

There are also safety concerns. Phones can be stolen, and cyberbullying can continue during school hours.

Some schools have found a middle path: phones stay in bags unless the teacher asks learners to use them for a task. This keeps the benefits while reducing distraction.

lesson.say: A summary gives only the main points of a text, in your own words, much shorter than the original.
lesson.html:
Main points→Own words→Short

No examples, no repetition, no opinions of your own.

lesson.say: Read the text. Underline one main point in each paragraph. Leave out examples and details. Rewrite the points in your own words. Check the word count.
lesson.html:
Read→Underline→Cut details→Rewrite→Count

Usually one point per paragraph.

lesson.say: Instead of: For learners without books at home, a phone may be their main way to research. Write: Phones help learners who have few books.
lesson.html:
Original: For learners without books at home, a phone may be their main way to research.

Summary point: Phones help learners with few books.

example.q: Summarise paragraph 4 in one point.
steps: Paragraph 4 is about safety.
Main idea: phones can be stolen and bullying continues.
Phones create safety risks.

questions.q: What should a summary include?
questions.explain: A summary includes only the main points.

questions.q: Which is the best summary of paragraph 3?
options: Phones distract learners and may lower results.
Notifications are sounds that phones make.
questions.explain: It captures distraction and lower results.

questions.q: Which should you leave out of a summary?
questions.explain: Specific examples are usually left out.

questions.q: Why use your own words?
options: It shows you understood the text
questions.explain: Rewording shows you understood it.

questions.q: Put the summary steps in order.
questions.explain: Read, underline, rewrite, check.

units.parent: Your child practised writing summaries by choosing main points and using their own words.
units.teacher: Shows selecting main ideas, excluding examples and rewording within a word limit.
units.done: A summary is short, in your own words, with only the main points.

units.subject: English Home Language
units.title: Subject-verb agreement
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 English Home Language: Language Structures and Conventions (concord: subject-verb agreement, including collective nouns and indefinite pronouns)
units.intention: Today I am making sure the verb agrees with its subject.
units.prompt: Which concord rule was new to you?

lesson.say: A singular subject takes a singular verb. A plural subject takes a plural verb. The dog barks. The dogs bark.
lesson.html:
The dog barks.→The dogs bark.

This is called concord.

lesson.say: Each, everyone, nobody and either are singular. Everyone is here. Each of the learners has a book.
lesson.html:
Everyone is→Each of them has→Nobody knows

Ignore the words between the subject and the verb: Each of the learners has.

lesson.say: A collective noun names a group, like team, class or family. When the group acts as one, use a singular verb. The team is winning.
lesson.html:
The team is→The class has→The committee decides

Neither … nor: the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

example.q: Choose the correct verb: The box of pencils (is / are) on the desk.
steps: What is the subject? The box, not the pencils.
Box is singular.
The box of pencils is on the desk.

questions.q: The learners … in the hall.
questions.explain: The learners are in the hall.

questions.q: Everyone … finished the test.
questions.explain: Everyone has finished.

questions.q: One of my friends … to Durban.
hints: What is the subject: one or friends?
questions.explain: One … is moving.

questions.q: The choir … practising for the festival.
hints: Choir is a collective noun acting as one.
questions.explain: The choir is practising.

questions.q: Neither the teacher nor the learners … ready.
questions.explain: The verb agrees with learners: were.

units.parent: Your child practised making verbs agree with their subjects.
units.teacher: Shows subject-verb concord with intervening phrases, indefinite pronouns, collective nouns and neither/nor.
units.done: Find the real subject, then match the verb to it.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: Cells, tissues and systems
units.topic: Cells as the basic units of life
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Natural Sciences, Term 1 Life and Living: Cells as the basic units of life (plant and animal cells; cells, tissues, organs and systems)
units.intention: Today I am comparing plant and animal cells, and how cells build body systems.
units.prompt: Why do plant cells need a cell wall?

lesson.say: All living things are made of cells. Most cells have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and a nucleus. The nucleus controls the cell.
lesson.html:
Membrane→Cytoplasm→Nucleus

A cell is the smallest unit of life.

lesson.say: Plant cells also have a cell wall for support, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a large vacuole. Animal cells do not have these.
lesson.html:
Plant only: cell wall→chloroplasts→large vacuole

That is why plants stand upright and are green.

lesson.say: Similar cells form tissues. Tissues form organs. Organs work together in systems. For example, muscle cells make muscle tissue, which forms the heart, part of the circulatory system.
lesson.html:
Cell→Tissue→Organ→System→Organism

Each level is built from the one before.

example.q: A cell has a cell wall and chloroplasts. Is it a plant or animal cell?
steps: Animal cells do not have cell walls or chloroplasts.
Plant cells have both.
It is a plant cell.

questions.q: Which part controls the cell?
questions.explain: The nucleus controls the cell.

questions.q: Which is found in plant cells but NOT animal cells?
hints: Animal cells have a membrane only.
questions.explain: Only plant cells have a cell wall.

questions.q: Put the levels in order, smallest first.
questions.explain: Cell, tissue, organ, system.

questions.q: Which organ belongs to the respiratory system?
questions.explain: The lungs are part of the respiratory system.

questions.q: What do chloroplasts do?
questions.explain: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.

units.parent: Your child compared plant and animal cells and learned how cells build tissues, organs and systems.
units.teacher: Shows identifying cell organelles, comparing plant and animal cells, and the levels of organisation.
units.done: Cells build tissues, organs and systems.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: Acids, bases and pH
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Natural Sciences, Term 2 Matter and Materials: Reactions of acids with bases (pH scale; indicators; neutralisation)
units.intention: Today I am using the pH scale to classify acids and bases.
units.prompt: Where do you find acids and bases at home?

lesson.say: The pH scale runs from zero to fourteen. Below seven is acidic. Seven is neutral, like pure water. Above seven is basic, also called alkaline.
lesson.html:
0–6 acid→7 neutral→8–14 base

Lemon juice is about pH 2. Soap is about pH 10.

lesson.say: An indicator changes colour to show whether something is acidic or basic. Litmus paper turns red in acid and blue in a base. Red cabbage juice also works.
lesson.html:
🟥 🟦

Acid: blue litmus turns red. Base: red litmus turns blue.

lesson.say: When an acid and a base react, they neutralise each other, making a salt and water. Antacid tablets neutralise extra stomach acid.
lesson.html:
acid + base→→→salt + water

This is called neutralisation.

example.q: A liquid turns blue litmus red. What is it?
steps: Blue litmus turns red in acid.
So the liquid is acidic.
Its pH is below 7.

questions.q: What pH is neutral?
questions.explain: pH 7 is neutral.

questions.q: Vinegar has a pH of about 3. What is it?
questions.explain: pH 3 is acidic.

questions.q: What does red litmus do in a base?
questions.explain: Bases turn red litmus blue.

questions.q: What do an acid and a base make when they react?
questions.explain: Acid + base → salt + water.

questions.q: Acid or base?
hints: Soap and bicarb feel slippery or bitter.
questions.explain: Lemon juice and vinegar are acids. Soap and bicarbonate are bases.

units.parent: Your child learned the pH scale, indicators and neutralisation.
units.teacher: Shows classifying substances by pH, interpreting indicator colours and describing neutralisation.
units.done: Acids are below pH 7, bases above. Together they neutralise.

units.subject: Natural Sciences
units.title: The rock cycle and mining
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Natural Sciences, Term 4 Planet Earth and Beyond: Lithosphere (Earth's layers; the rock cycle; mining and refining minerals; environmental impacts of mining)
units.intention: Today I am learning how rocks form and change, and how mining affects the environment.
units.prompt: How could mining be made less harmful?

lesson.say: Igneous rock forms when hot magma or lava cools, like granite. Sedimentary rock forms when layers of sand and mud are pressed together, like sandstone. Metamorphic rock forms when heat and pressure change rock, like marble.
lesson.html:
Igneous: cooled magma→Sedimentary: layers→Metamorphic: changed

Table Mountain's top is mostly sandstone.

lesson.say: Rocks change from one type to another over millions of years. Weathering breaks rock into sediment. Heat and pressure change it. Melting turns it into magma again.
lesson.html:
Weathering→Sediment→Pressure→Heat→Melting→Cooling

The rock cycle never stops.

lesson.say: South Africa mines gold, platinum, coal, iron ore and diamonds. Mining creates jobs, but it can damage land, pollute water and harm workers' health. Mines must rehabilitate land when they close.
lesson.html:
⛏️ 💎 🏭

Weigh economic benefits against environmental costs.

example.q: Lava from a volcano cools into black rock. What type of rock is it?
steps: It formed from cooling molten rock.
Cooled magma or lava makes igneous rock.
It is igneous rock.

questions.q: Which rock forms from layers of sediment pressed together?
questions.explain: Sedimentary rock forms from compressed layers.

questions.q: Marble forms when limestone is changed by heat and pressure. What type is marble?
questions.explain: Marble is metamorphic.

questions.q: What breaks rocks into small pieces?
questions.explain: Weathering breaks rocks into sediment.

questions.q: Which is an environmental impact of mining?
questions.explain: Acid mine drainage can pollute water.

questions.q: What does rehabilitating a mine mean?
options: Restoring the land after mining ends
questions.explain: Mines must restore the land when they close.

units.parent: Your child learned about igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, the rock cycle and mining's impact.
units.teacher: Shows classifying rock types, describing the rock cycle and evaluating the impacts of mining.
units.done: Rocks change through the rock cycle. Mining has benefits and costs.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Choosing Grade 10 subjects
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Life Orientation: World of work (subject choice for Grade 10 to 12; career and study pathways; requirements for further study)
units.intention: Today I am learning how to choose subjects for Grade 10 to 12.
units.prompt: Which subjects are you thinking of, and why?

lesson.say: In Grades 10 to 12 you take seven subjects. Four are compulsory: a home language, a first additional language, Mathematics or Mathematical Literacy, and Life Orientation. You choose the other three.
lesson.html:
2 languages→Maths or Maths Lit→Life Orientation→3 choices

The three choices can be academic, technical or occupational, depending on your school.

lesson.say: Many university courses in science, engineering, medicine and commerce require Mathematics, not Mathematical Literacy. Check before you choose.
lesson.html:
Engineering: Maths→Medicine: Maths + Physical Sciences→Many arts courses: either

This choice opens or closes some doors.

lesson.say: Think about what you enjoy, what you are good at, and what careers you are curious about. Look up entry requirements, and talk to your teachers and family.
lesson.html:
Interests→Strengths→Career requirements→Advice

Universities and TVET colleges list admission requirements online.

example.q: Lerato wants to study engineering. Which subjects should she take?
steps: Engineering usually requires Mathematics.
It also usually requires Physical Sciences.
She should take Mathematics and Physical Sciences, and check the university's requirements.

questions.q: How many subjects do learners take in Grades 10 to 12?
hints: Two languages, maths, LO and three more.
questions.explain: Seven subjects.

questions.q: Which subject is compulsory?
questions.explain: Life Orientation is compulsory.

questions.q: Someone who wants to become a doctor should usually take …
questions.explain: Medicine usually requires Mathematics and Physical Sciences.

questions.q: Where can you find a course's admission requirements?
questions.explain: Check the institution's official website.

questions.q: What is the best reason to choose a subject?
options: It fits your interests, strengths and goals
questions.explain: Choose based on your interests, strengths and goals.

units.parent: Your child learned how Grade 10 to 12 subject choices link to careers and study. A good time to talk together about options.
units.teacher: Shows knowledge of FET subject packages, the Maths or Maths Literacy decision and researching admission requirements.
units.done: Choose subjects that match your interests, strengths and goals, and check the requirements.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Setting SMART goals
units.topic: Development of the self: goal setting
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Life Orientation: Development of the self in society (goal-setting skills; personal lifestyle plan; time management)
units.intention: Today I am turning a wish into a SMART goal.
units.prompt: What is one goal you want to set this term?

lesson.h: A wish is not a goal
lesson.say: I want to do better at maths is a wish. A goal is clear and has a plan. SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
lesson.html:
Specific→Measurable→Achievable→Relevant→Time-bound

SMART turns a wish into a plan.

lesson.say: Wish: get better at maths. SMART goal: I will improve my maths mark from 55 to 65 percent by the end of term. I will do 20 minutes of practice every weekday.
lesson.html: I will improve my maths mark from 55% to 65% by the end of term, by doing 20 minutes of practice every weekday.

lesson.say: Break the goal into small steps. Track your progress. If you have a setback, adjust the plan, not the dream.
lesson.html:
Small steps→Track→Adjust

Setbacks are information, not failure.

example.q: Make this SMART: I want to get fit.
steps: Specific: run.
Measurable and time-bound: run 3 kilometres without stopping in 8 weeks.
Plan: run three times a week, adding a little each week.

questions.q: What does the M in SMART stand for?
hints: You can count or check it.
questions.explain: M is for measurable.

questions.q: Which goal is SMART?
options: Read two books by 30 June, 20 pages a day
Read every book in the library
hints: Which is specific and has a date?
questions.explain: It is specific, measurable and has a deadline.

questions.q: Why break a goal into small steps?
questions.explain: Small steps make big goals manageable.

questions.q: Score 100% in every test this year, starting tomorrow. Which part of SMART is weak?
hints: Perfect every time is very hard.
questions.explain: It may not be achievable.

questions.q: You miss your weekly target. What is a helpful response?
options: Adjust the plan and keep going
questions.explain: Adjust the plan and keep going.

reflect.q: Which part of SMART is hardest for you?

units.parent: Your child learned to set SMART goals and plan steps towards them.
units.teacher: Shows applying the SMART framework, breaking goals into steps and responding constructively to setbacks.
units.done: SMART goals are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

units.subject: Life Orientation
units.title: Making a difference in your community
units.caps: CAPS Grade 9 Life Orientation: Social and environmental responsibility (community and environmental problems; volunteering; planning a community project)
units.intention: Today I am planning a small project to help my community.
units.prompt: What problem in your community would you like to help solve?

lesson.say: Look around your community. Is there litter, a lack of safe play spaces, learners who need help reading, or a water problem?
lesson.html:
🗑️ 📚 💧 🌳

Start with a problem you care about.

lesson.say: Decide the goal, who will help, what you need, what it will cost, and when it will happen. Ask permission where needed.
lesson.html:
Goal→Team→Resources→Timeline→Permission

A small, finished project beats a big, unfinished one.

lesson.say: Carry out the project. Afterwards, ask: what worked, what did not, and what changed in the community?
lesson.html:
Act→Measure→Reflect

Count the impact: bags collected, children helped, trees planted.

example.q: Learners notice litter near the school gate. What could a project look like?
steps: Goal: clean the area and keep it clean.
Plan: a Saturday clean-up with gloves and bags, permission from the principal, and bins from the municipality.
Reflect: count the bags, take before and after photos, and check a month later.

questions.q: What is the first step in a community project?
questions.explain: Start by identifying a real need.

questions.q: Why ask permission before a project?
options: To work safely and with support
questions.explain: Permission keeps the project safe and supported.

questions.q: Which is a measurable result?
questions.explain: 35 bags is measurable.

questions.q: What does volunteering mean?
options: Giving your time to help without being paid
questions.explain: Volunteering is helping by choice, without pay.

questions.q: Put the project steps in order.
questions.explain: Need, plan, act, reflect.

reflect.q: Which kind of project interests you?

units.parent: Your child planned a community project, from spotting a need to measuring the impact.
units.teacher: Shows identifying community needs, planning a project with resources and permissions, and evaluating impact.
units.done: Spot a need, plan carefully, act, and measure your impact.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Pythagoras' theorem
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics (0862), Stage 9: Geometry and measure (Pythagoras' theorem in two dimensions)
units.intention: Today I am using Pythagoras' theorem to find missing sides.
units.prompt: How long is the diagonal of a soccer field?

lesson.say: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.
lesson.html: a² + b² = c²

lesson.say: If the two shorter sides are 3 and 4, then c squared is 9 plus 16, which is 25. So c is 5.
To find a shorter side, subtract. If c is 13 and a is 5, then b squared is 169 minus 25, which is 144, so b is 12.

example.q: A ladder 10 m long leans against a wall with its foot 6 m from the wall. How high up the wall does it reach?
steps: The ladder is the hypotenuse: 10 m.
h = 8 m.

questions.q: The two shorter sides are 6 and 8. Find the hypotenuse.
The hypotenuse is 13 and one side is 12. Find the other side.
Which side is the hypotenuse?
options: The longest side, opposite the right angle
questions.explain: It is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.

questions.q: Do the sides 5, 12 and 13 make a right-angled triangle?
A rectangle is 9 cm by 12 cm. How long is its diagonal, in cm?

units.parent: Your child used Pythagoras' theorem to find missing sides.
units.teacher: Shows applying Pythagoras' theorem to find the hypotenuse and shorter sides, and testing for right angles.
units.done: a² + b² = c²: add to find the hypotenuse, subtract to find a shorter side.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Probability and expected frequency
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics (0862), Stage 9: Statistics and probability (relative frequency; expected frequency; comparing with theoretical probability)
units.intention: Today I am predicting how often an event should happen.
units.prompt: If you toss a coin 100 times, will you get exactly 50 heads?

lesson.say: Expected frequency is the probability times the number of trials. Rolling a dice 60 times, you expect a 6 about 1 sixth of 60, which is 10 times.
lesson.html: Expected frequency = P(event) × number of trials

lesson.say: Relative frequency is how often something actually happened, divided by the number of trials. If you got 12 sixes in 60 rolls, the relative frequency is 12 over 60, or 0.2.
lesson.html: Relative frequency = times it happened ÷ trials

lesson.say: With many trials, relative frequency should be close to the theoretical probability. A big difference after many trials may suggest the dice is biased.
lesson.html: More trials → more reliable estimate

example.q: A spinner has P(red) = 0.25. It is spun 200 times. How many reds do you expect?
steps: Expected = P × trials.
= 50 reds.

questions.q: A coin is tossed 80 times. How many heads do you expect?
A dice is rolled 120 times. How many 3s do you expect?
A drawing pin lands point-up 30 times in 50 throws. What is the relative frequency of point-up?
A dice lands on 6 in 300 of 600 rolls. What might this suggest?
questions.explain: 300 is far more than the expected 100, so it may be biased.

questions.q: Why is a relative frequency from 1 000 trials more reliable than from 10?
options: More trials give a better estimate of the true probability
questions.explain: With more trials, results get closer to the true probability.

units.parent: Your child predicted results using probability and compared them with experiments.
units.teacher: Shows calculating expected and relative frequency and interpreting differences from theoretical probability.
units.done: Expected = P × trials. Relative frequency = times ÷ trials.

units.subject: English
units.title: How texts are structured
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary English (1111), Stage 9: Reading (how writers structure non-fiction texts for effect)
units.intention: Today I am analysing how a writer structures a text.
units.prompt: Why do news reports put the most important facts first?
units.passage:
Should our town ban plastic bags? (a 2to.iQ article)

Plastic bags are cheap, light and useful, which is exactly the problem: we use them for minutes and throw them away. In our town, volunteers removed more than 3 000 bags from the river last year.

However, a ban is not simple. Some small shop owners say paper bags cost them five times as much, and some families reuse plastic bags as bin liners.

A charge for each bag may be a fairer first step. Where shops have charged for bags, many shoppers have switched to bags they can reuse.

lesson.say: Read the text, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Should our town ban plastic bags? (a 2to.iQ article)

Plastic bags are cheap, light and useful, which is exactly the problem: we use them for minutes and throw them away. In our town, volunteers removed more than 3 000 bags from the river last year.

However, a ban is not simple. Some small shop owners say paper bags cost them five times as much, and some families reuse plastic bags as bin liners.

A charge for each bag may be a fairer first step. Where shops have charged for bags, many shoppers have switched to bags they can reuse.

lesson.say: Writers decide what goes first, in the middle and last. This article opens with the problem, then gives the other side, and ends with a solution.
lesson.html: Problem→Complication→Solution

lesson.say: The opening hooks the reader with a surprising idea: plastic bags are useful, and that is exactly the problem. The ending leaves the reader with a possible way forward.
lesson.html: Opening: hook. Ending: resolution.

example.q: Why does the writer put the river statistic in the first paragraph?
steps: It gives evidence of the problem early.
A concrete number makes the problem real.
It hooks the reader before the complications.

questions.q: How does the article begin?
options: With a surprising statement about why bags are a problem
With a story about a shop
questions.explain: It opens by turning the bags' usefulness into the problem.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the second paragraph?
options: To present complications with a ban
questions.explain: It shows why a ban is not simple.

questions.q: Why does the writer end with a possible solution?
options: To leave the reader with a way forward
Because they ran out of words
questions.explain: It resolves the tension the article built up.

questions.q: Which structure does the article follow?
questions.explain: Problem → complication → solution.

questions.q: Which is the best comment on structure?
options: By moving from problem to complication to solution, the writer guides the reader towards the bag charge.
questions.explain: It explains how the structure guides the reader.

options: Looking at the opening and ending

units.parent: Your child analysed how the structure of an article guides the reader.
units.teacher: Shows analysing the function of paragraphs and the effect of structural choices in non-fiction.
units.done: Ask what each part does, and how the order guides the reader.

units.subject: English
units.title: Writing a speech
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary English (1111), Stage 9: Writing and speaking (writing and delivering a persuasive speech for an audience)
units.intention: Today I am writing a speech that persuades an audience.
units.prompt: What makes a speaker worth listening to?

lesson.say: A speech is written to be heard. So use short sentences. Speak directly to the audience with you and we. Use clear signpost words like firstly and finally.
lesson.html: Short sentences→You and we→Signposts

lesson.say: Speakers use the rule of three, rhetorical questions and repetition to make ideas memorable. For example: we can recycle, we can reuse, we can refuse.
lesson.html: We can recycle. We can reuse. We can refuse.

lesson.say: End with a call to action that tells the audience exactly what to do next.
lesson.html: 'Bring one reusable bag tomorrow. That's all it takes to start.'

example.q: Write an opening line for a speech about saving water.
steps: Hook the audience directly.
Use a question or a striking fact.
'What would you do if you turned on the tap tomorrow and nothing came out?'

questions.q: Why do speeches use 'you' and 'we'?
questions.explain: Direct address makes the audience feel involved.

questions.q: 'We can recycle, we can reuse, we can refuse' uses…
options: the rule of three and repetition
questions.explain: Three parallel ideas with a repeated phrase.

questions.q: Which is a rhetorical question?
options: 'Do we really want our children to inherit a dirty river?'
questions.explain: It makes a point rather than asking for information.

questions.q: Which ending is a clear call to action?
questions.explain: It tells the audience exactly what to do.

questions.q: Why are short sentences useful in a speech?
options: They are easier for listeners to follow
questions.explain: Listeners follow short sentences more easily.

units.parent: Your child practised writing a persuasive speech.
units.teacher: Shows adapting writing for spoken delivery, using rhetorical devices and crafting a call to action.
units.done: Write for the ear: short, direct, memorable, with a clear call to action.

units.subject: Science
units.title: The reactivity of metals
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (0893), Stage 9: Chemistry (the reactivity series; displacement reactions)
units.intention: Today I am ordering metals by how reactive they are.
units.prompt: Why do iron gates rust but gold rings don't?

lesson.say: Metals can be put in order of how readily they react. Potassium and sodium are very reactive. Gold and silver hardly react at all.
lesson.html:
Potassium→Sodium→Magnesium→Zinc→Iron→Copper→Gold

Most reactive → least reactive

lesson.say: More reactive metals react faster with acids and water, giving off hydrogen gas. Magnesium fizzes quickly in acid; copper doesn't react with dilute acid.
lesson.html: metal + acid → salt + hydrogen

lesson.say: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from a solution of its compound. Iron placed in copper sulfate becomes coated in copper.
lesson.html: iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper

example.q: Will zinc displace copper from copper sulfate solution?
steps: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one.
Yes: zinc sulfate and copper are formed.

questions.q: Which metal is most reactive?
questions.explain: Potassium is at the top of the series.

questions.q: What gas is given off when magnesium reacts with acid?
questions.explain: Metals and acids produce hydrogen.

questions.q: Will copper displace iron from iron sulfate?
options: No, copper is less reactive than iron
questions.explain: A less reactive metal can't displace a more reactive one.

questions.q: Why is gold used for jewellery?
options: It is very unreactive, so it doesn't tarnish
questions.explain: Gold's low reactivity keeps it shiny.

questions.q: Iron is placed in copper sulfate solution. What do you see?
questions.explain: Iron displaces copper, which coats the iron.

units.parent: Your child ordered metals by reactivity and predicted reactions.
units.teacher: Shows using the reactivity series to predict reactions with acids and displacement reactions.
units.done: Higher in the series means more reactive, and it can displace metals below it.

units.subject: Science
units.title: The carbon cycle and climate
units.caps: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science (0893), Stage 9: Earth and space (the carbon cycle; the greenhouse effect; human impact on climate)
units.intention: Today I am tracing carbon through the carbon cycle.
units.prompt: Where does the carbon in a burning log go?

lesson.say: Carbon moves between the air, living things, the oceans and rocks. Plants take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. Respiration, decay and burning release it.
lesson.html: Photosynthesis: takes CO₂ in→Respiration, decay, burning: give CO₂ out

lesson.say: Carbon dioxide and some other gases trap heat in the atmosphere, keeping Earth warm enough for life. More of these gases trap more heat.
lesson.html: More greenhouse gases → more heat trapped

lesson.say: Burning fossil fuels and cutting down forests add carbon dioxide to the air faster than it is removed. This is causing global temperatures to rise.
lesson.html: Burning fossil fuels→Deforestation→More CO₂→Warming

example.q: Explain how cutting down forests increases carbon dioxide in the air.
steps: Trees remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis.
Fewer trees means less carbon dioxide is removed.
If the trees are burnt, their stored carbon is released too.

questions.q: Which process removes carbon dioxide from the air?
hints: They use CO₂ to make glucose.
questions.explain: Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide in.

questions.q: Which process releases carbon dioxide?
questions.explain: Burning releases carbon dioxide.

questions.q: What does the greenhouse effect do?
questions.explain: Greenhouse gases trap heat.

questions.q: Why is the greenhouse effect needed for life?
options: Without it, Earth would be too cold
questions.explain: Some trapped heat keeps Earth warm enough for life.

questions.q: Which action would reduce carbon dioxide in the air?
questions.explain: More trees remove more carbon dioxide.

units.parent: Your child traced carbon through the carbon cycle and linked it to climate change.
units.teacher: Shows describing processes in the carbon cycle, explaining the greenhouse effect and evaluating human impact.
units.done: Photosynthesis takes carbon dioxide in; respiration, decay and burning release it.

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Linear models
units.caps: IB MYP Mathematics, year 4: Algebra (linear functions as models). Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Globalization and sustainability.
units.intention: Today I am using straight-line equations to model real situations.
units.prompt: How could you predict next month's water bill?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Modelling relationships between quantities helps us make sustainable choices. Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Globalization and sustainability.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Modelling relationships between quantities helps us make sustainable choices.

Key concept: Relationships · Global context: Globalization and sustainability

lesson.say: Many costs have a fixed part and a part that grows at a steady rate. A water bill of 50 dollars a month plus 2 dollars per kilolitre is C equals 2k plus 50.
lesson.html: C = 2k + 50: 2 is the rate, 50 is the fixed cost

lesson.say: Use the model to predict, then ask whether it is realistic. Many cities charge more per kilolitre for heavy users, so a straight line may stop fitting.
lesson.html: Every model has limits.

example.q: Using C = 2k + 50, what do 15 kilolitres cost?
steps: Substitute k = 15: C = 2(15) + 50.

questions.q: Using C = 2k + 50, find the cost of 10 kL, in dollars.
In C = 2k + 50, what does 50 represent?
hints: You pay it even with no water.
questions.explain: 50 is paid whatever you use: the fixed cost.

questions.q: A taxi charges $3 plus $1.50 per km. What does a 6 km trip cost, in dollars?
A gym charges $20 to join and $15 per month. Which equation models the cost for m months?
questions.explain: Rate $15 per month, fixed $20: C = 15m + 20.

questions.q: A city charges more per kilolitre above 20 kL. What does this mean for the straight-line model?
hints: A straight line has one rate.
questions.explain: The rate changes above 20 kL, so one straight line no longer fits.

options: Finding the rate and the fixed part

units.parent: Your child used straight-line equations to model costs, and judged where a model stops working.
units.teacher: Criterion D (applying mathematics in real-life contexts): constructs and uses linear models, interprets parameters and evaluates a model's limits.
units.done: Rate × amount + fixed cost. Then ask: is the model realistic?

units.subject: Mathematics
units.title: Similar shapes and scale
units.caps: IB MYP Mathematics, year 4: Geometry (similarity and scale factors). Key concept: Form. Global context: Personal and cultural expression.
units.intention: Today I am using scale factors with similar shapes and models.
units.prompt: How do architects show a building before it is built?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: The form of an object can be scaled while keeping its proportions. This lets artists and architects plan their work. Key concept: Form. Global context: Personal and cultural expression.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: The form of an object can be scaled while keeping its proportions. This lets artists and architects plan their work.

Key concept: Form · Global context: Personal and cultural expression

lesson.say: Two shapes are similar if one is an enlargement of the other. The angles are the same. Every length is multiplied by the same scale factor.
lesson.html: Scale factor = new length ÷ original length

lesson.say: Architects build scale models. In a 1 to 50 model, every real length is 50 times the model length.
lesson.html: Model 1 : 50 → 4 cm on the model = 200 cm = 2 m real

example.q: A photo 10 cm wide is enlarged to 25 cm wide. It was 8 cm high. Find the new height.
steps: Scale factor = 25 ÷ 10 = 2.5.
New height = 8 × 2.5.

questions.q: A rectangle 4 cm by 6 cm is enlarged by scale factor 3. How long is the 6 cm side now, in cm?
A 5 cm side becomes 15 cm. What is the scale factor?
Two triangles are similar. Which must be true?
questions.explain: Similar shapes have equal angles; lengths are in proportion.

questions.q: A model is 1 : 50. A wall is 6 cm long on the model. How long is it really, in metres?
A sculpture is enlarged by scale factor 2. What happens to its angles?
questions.explain: Angles don't change in an enlargement.

units.parent: Your child worked with similar shapes, scale factors and scale models.
units.teacher: Criterion A (knowing and understanding): identifies similar figures and applies scale factors to lengths and models.
units.done: Similar: the same angles, and lengths × the same scale factor.

units.subject: Language and Literature
units.title: Point of view
units.caps: IB MYP Language and Literature, year 4: Criterion A, Analysing (narrative point of view and its effect). Key concept: Perspective. Global context: Identities and relationships.
units.intention: Today I am analysing how point of view changes a story.
units.prompt: How would your day sound told by someone else?
units.passage:
Version 1

I hate Saturdays at the stall. Ma says smile, so I smile, but my feet ache and every customer wants change for a R200 note. When Thabo from school walks past, I duck behind the tomatoes.

Version 2

Every Saturday, Naledi helped her mother at the vegetable stall. She smiled at the customers and counted their change carefully. When a boy from her class walked past, she suddenly became very interested in the tomatoes.

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: The perspective a writer chooses shapes how readers understand a character's identity. Key concept: Perspective. Global context: Identities and relationships.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: The perspective a writer chooses shapes how readers understand a character's identity.

Key concept: Perspective · Global context: Identities and relationships

lesson.say: Read the text, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
Version 1

I hate Saturdays at the stall. Ma says smile, so I smile, but my feet ache and every customer wants change for a R200 note. When Thabo from school walks past, I duck behind the tomatoes.

Version 2

Every Saturday, Naledi helped her mother at the vegetable stall. She smiled at the customers and counted their change carefully. When a boy from her class walked past, she suddenly became very interested in the tomatoes.

lesson.say: Version 1 is in the first person: the narrator says I, and we hear her private thoughts. Version 2 is in the third person: the narrator says she, and we watch from outside.
lesson.html: First person: I, my→Third person: she, he, they

lesson.say: First person feels close and honest: we know she hates Saturdays. Third person gives distance: we have to infer her feelings from what she does, such as hiding behind the tomatoes.
lesson.html: Ask: what do we know, and how do we know it?

example.q: What does 'she suddenly became very interested in the tomatoes' suggest?
steps: She is not really interested in tomatoes.
She is avoiding the boy from her class.
The narrator hints at her embarrassment with gentle humour.

questions.q: Which version is written in the first person?
questions.explain: Version 1 uses 'I'.

questions.q: What do we learn directly in Version 1 that we must infer in Version 2?
options: That she dislikes working at the stall
hints: Which feeling is stated in Version 1?
questions.explain: Version 1 states her dislike; Version 2 never does.

questions.q: Why might a writer choose the first person?
options: To let readers share the character's private thoughts
questions.explain: First person lets us inside the narrator's head.

questions.q: What is the effect of 'I duck behind the tomatoes'?
options: It shows her embarrassment directly, with humour
questions.explain: Hiding shows her embarrassment in a funny, honest way.

questions.q: Which pronoun shows third-person narration?
hints: Third person is outside the character.
questions.explain: 'She' shows third person.

units.parent: Your child analysed how telling a story as 'I' or 'she' changes what readers know.
units.teacher: Criterion A: analyses how narrative point of view shapes characterisation and the reader's response.
units.done: Point of view decides what we know and how close we feel.

units.subject: Language and Literature
units.title: Analysing an advertisement
units.caps: IB MYP Language and Literature, year 4: Criterion A, Analysing (persuasive techniques and audience in media texts). Key concept: Communication. Global context: Globalization and sustainability.
units.intention: Today I am analysing how an advert persuades, and questioning its claims.
units.prompt: Which advert have you seen that you didn't believe?
units.passage:
FRESHA bottled water (a made-up advert)

Pure. Natural. You.

Drawn from ancient mountain springs, FRESHA is the choice of champions. 9 out of 10 athletes we asked prefer it. Why settle for ordinary when you could be extraordinary?

Now in new 100% recycled bottles.*

*Cap and label not included.

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Advertisers communicate with carefully chosen audiences, and critical readers question the claims they make. Key concept: Communication. Global context: Globalization and sustainability.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Advertisers communicate with carefully chosen audiences, and critical readers question the claims they make.

Key concept: Communication · Global context: Globalization and sustainability

lesson.say: Read the text, or press Read aloud to hear it part by part.
lesson.html:
FRESHA bottled water (a made-up advert)

Pure. Natural. You.

Drawn from ancient mountain springs, FRESHA is the choice of champions. 9 out of 10 athletes we asked prefer it. Why settle for ordinary when you could be extraordinary?

Now in new 100% recycled bottles.*

*Cap and label not included.

lesson.say: Adverts use many techniques. They use short slogans, statistics and rhetorical questions. They appeal to who the reader is, or link the product with nature or success.
lesson.html: Slogan→Statistic→Rhetorical question→Association

lesson.say: Ask who made the advert, who it is for, and what it leaves out. Small print often limits a big claim.
lesson.html: Check the small print and the sample.

example.q: Analyse '9 out of 10 athletes we asked prefer it'.
steps: It is a statistic, which sounds scientific.
'We asked' means the company chose whom to ask, and we don't know how many.
It persuades by linking the water with athletes, but the evidence is weak.

questions.q: Who is the target audience?
options: People who want to feel healthy and successful
hints: Who wants to feel like that?
questions.explain: The advert appeals to people who want health and success.

questions.q: 'Why settle for ordinary when you could be extraordinary?' is…
questions.explain: It is a question asked for effect.

questions.q: What does the small print reveal?
options: The 100% recycled claim isn't true of the whole bottle
hints: So not all of it is recycled.
questions.explain: The cap and label aren't recycled, so the claim is limited.

questions.q: Why is '9 out of 10 athletes we asked' weak evidence?
options: We don't know how many were asked or how they were chosen
questions.explain: The sample size and selection are unknown.

questions.q: 'Pure. Natural. You.' links the product with…
questions.explain: It suggests the water is part of who you are.

options: Asking who the advert is for

units.parent: Your child analysed how an advert persuades and questioned its claims.
units.teacher: Criterion A: analyses persuasive techniques, audience and purpose, and evaluates the reliability of claims in media texts.
units.done: Name the technique, find the audience, and question the claim.

units.subject: Sciences
units.title: Designing a fair test
units.caps: IB MYP Sciences, year 4: Criterion B, Inquiring and designing (hypotheses, variables and fair testing). Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Scientific and technical innovation.
units.intention: Today I am planning a fair scientific investigation.
units.prompt: How could you test which washing powder works best?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Scientists test relationships between variables by changing one thing at a time. Key concept: Relationships. Global context: Scientific and technical innovation.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Scientists test relationships between variables by changing one thing at a time.

Key concept: Relationships · Global context: Scientific and technical innovation

lesson.say: The independent variable is what you change. The dependent variable is what you measure. Control variables are kept the same, so the test is fair.
lesson.html: Change: independent→Measure: dependent→Keep the same: controls

lesson.say: A hypothesis predicts the relationship and gives a scientific reason. For example: if the water is warmer, then sugar will dissolve faster, because the particles move faster.
lesson.html: If … then … because …

lesson.say: Repeat each trial at least three times and calculate a mean, so one odd result doesn't mislead you.
lesson.html: Repeat, then find the mean.

example.q: Plan: does the amount of light affect how tall bean plants grow?
steps: Independent: hours of light each day.
Dependent: plant height after two weeks.
Controls: the same water, soil, pot size and type of bean.

questions.q: You test how ramp height affects a toy car's speed. What is the independent variable?
hints: What do you change on purpose?
questions.explain: You change the ramp height.

questions.q: In the same test, what is the dependent variable?
questions.explain: You measure the car's speed.

questions.q: Why must control variables stay the same?
options: So any change is caused only by the independent variable
questions.explain: Keeping controls the same means you know what caused the change.

questions.q: Which is the best hypothesis?
options: If the water is warmer, then the sugar will dissolve faster, because the particles move faster.
questions.explain: It predicts a relationship and gives a scientific reason.

questions.q: Why repeat each trial three times?
options: To spot odd results and make the data more reliable
hints: One result could be a mistake.
questions.explain: Repeats reveal odd results and make the mean more reliable.

options: Naming the three kinds of variable

units.parent: Your child planned a fair investigation with a hypothesis and controlled variables.
units.teacher: Criterion B: formulates testable hypotheses with scientific reasoning, identifies variables and designs a fair, repeatable method.
units.done: Change one thing, measure one thing, keep the rest the same, and repeat.

units.subject: Sciences
units.title: Energy in ecosystems
units.caps: IB MYP Sciences, year 4: Biology (food chains and webs; energy transfer between trophic levels). Key concept: Systems. Global context: Globalization and sustainability.
units.intention: Today I am tracing how energy flows through an ecosystem.
units.prompt: What would happen if all the bees disappeared?

lesson.say: Statement of inquiry: Ecosystems are systems in which energy flows and matter cycles; human actions can upset their balance. Key concept: Systems. Global context: Globalization and sustainability.
lesson.html:
Statement of inquiry: Ecosystems are systems in which energy flows and matter cycles; human actions can upset their balance.

Key concept: Systems · Global context: Globalization and sustainability

lesson.say: A food chain shows what eats what. Energy flows from producers, such as grass, to consumers, such as a springbok and then a lion.
lesson.html: Grass (producer)→Springbok→Lion

lesson.say: Only about 10 percent of the energy at one level passes to the next. The rest is used for living or lost as heat. That is why food chains are short.
lesson.html: 1 000 kJ in grass → about 100 kJ in springbok → about 10 kJ in lion

lesson.say: Removing one species affects others in the food web. If lions are removed, springbok numbers may grow and they may overgraze the grass.
lesson.html: Every link matters.

example.q: Grass stores 5 000 kJ. Using the 10% rule, about how much reaches the springbok?
steps: About 10% passes to the next level.
About 500 kJ reaches the springbok.

questions.q: What is the producer in grass → springbok → lion?
questions.explain: Grass makes food by photosynthesis.

questions.q: A producer stores 2 000 kJ. Using the 10% rule, about how much passes to the primary consumer, in kJ?
Where does most of the energy at each level go?
options: It is used for living or lost as heat
It goes back to the sun
questions.explain: Most is used in life processes and lost as heat.

questions.q: Lions are removed from an area. What might happen first?
questions.explain: Without predators, springbok numbers rise.

questions.q: Why are food chains rarely longer than four or five levels?
options: Too little energy is left at the top
hints: About 90% is lost at each step.
questions.explain: So much energy is lost that little remains for higher levels.

units.parent: Your child traced how energy flows through food chains, and what happens when the balance is upset.
units.teacher: Criterion A: explains energy flow in ecosystems, applies the 10% rule and predicts the effects of disturbance in a food web.
units.done: Energy flows up the chain, but about 90% is lost at each step.
